legend: Prostatic mucinous adenocarcinoma. Gleason pattern 3 adenocarcinoma composed of discrete glands with abundant extraluminal mucin.
Prostatic mucinous adenocarcinoma. Gleason pattern 4 adenocarcinoma composed of cribriform glands with extraluminal mucin.
Acinar adenocarcinoma with perineural invasion. Adenocarcinoma glands encircling a nerve.

Acinar adenocarcinoma with mucinous fibroplasia. Mucinous fibroplasia (or collagenous micronodule) is characterized by delicate loose eosinophilic fibrous tissue with an ingrowth of fibroblasts that impinge on glandular lumina.

Acinar adenocarcinoma with glomerulation. The glomerulation consists of a prostatic gland with a cribriform tuft attached to only one edge of the gland, resulting in a structure resembling a glomerulus.
Glomerulations consist of prostatic glands with a cribriform tuft attached to only one edge of the gland, resulting in a structure resembling a glomerulus.

diagnosis: Pleomorphic giant cell adenocarcinoma of the prostate
legend: This is from a recent case of a lymph node metastasis accompanying a radical prostatectomy, which was also metastatic to the penis at the time of surgery. Morphologically, it is a very high-grade carcinoma and contains a high degree of nuclear pleomorphism and many bizarre giant cells (shown here). Immunophenotypically, many of the tumour cells (including giant cells) were positive for PSA, and the lesion was diffusely positive for NKX3-1 and AR.

Prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN)-like carcinoma. This subtype of acinar adenocarcinoma comprises large, discrete glands with flat or tufted pseudostratified epithelium. Like in this case, the nuclei are often elongated, resembling those in ductal adenocarcinoma.

Signet-ring cell–like adenocarcinoma. This subtype of acinar adenocarcinoma shows numerous malignant cells with cytoplasmic vacuoles compressing the nucleus. This example is Gleason score 5 + 5 = 10.

Prostate biopsies were double-stained by immunofluorescence for ANXA3 (green; a marker of low WHO/ISUP grade group and normal tissue) and AMACR (P504S) (red; a marker of prostate cancer). The slides were scored using a Pathfinder reader-analyser, for quantitative digital pathology automated scanning; using a specialized algorithm, the Pathfinder software analysed the detected fluorescent signals to assign a specific Gleason score.

title: Gleason grade patterns (after the ISUP 2005 and 2014 modifications {16096414; 26492179})
tablehtml:
Gleason pattern

Key morphological features

Comments

1 and 2

Discrete regular glands; circumscribed, rounded nodules

Not used for needle biopsy specimens; very rarely used in grading radical prostatectomy specimens

3

Discrete glands with marked variation in size and shape; infiltration between non-neoplastic acini

Includes pseudohyperplastic, atrophic, and microcystic patterns

No longer includes cribriform or glomeruloid glands after the ISUP 2005 and 2014 consensus conferences

4

Fused microacinar glands, poorly formed glands without well-defined lumina, cribriform glands, or glomeruloid glands

 

5

Minimal glandular differentiation, comprising solid sheets, cords, small solid cylinders, or single cells

OR

Solid, cribriform or papillary structures with central necrosis (comedocarcinoma)

Most (but not all) comedocarcinomas are now recognized as IDC-P {30720899; 29878934}

IDC-P, intraductal carcinoma of the prostate; ISUP, International Society of Urological Pathology.

aFor core needle biopsies with multiple specimens there is uncertainty about whether the highest specimen score or the global (overall) Gleason score is superior in predicting the radical prostatectomy score and clinical outcome. ISUP recommends reporting a separate Gleason score for each biopsy site. Global scores should be assigned for each MRI-targeted lesion {32459716; 32589068}. bMost radical prostatectomy specimens show multifocal carcinoma {12137824}, and ISUP recommends that the Gleason scores of the largest, highest-grade, and highest-stage nodules are recorded. cISUP 2019 recommendations would allow assignment of a minor Gleason pattern 4 or 5 in a 3 + 3 = 6 (GG1) carcinoma provided that the pattern 4 or 5 represents ≤ 5% of the tumour volume. Genitourinary Pathology Society (GUPS) 2020 defines a minor tertiary pattern as requiring the presence of three different patterns, and confines its use to GG2 or GG3 cancers. Thus, in the GUPS system, a carcinoma with 96% pattern 3 and 4% pattern 4 would be scored as 3 + 4 = 7. dMinor tertiary grade patterns should be mentioned in the report. However, if tertiary pattern 5 constitutes > 5% of the tumour volume it becomes the secondary pattern in the Gleason score (i.e. either 3 + 5 = 8 or 4 + 5 = 9). eA cancer scored as 4 + 4 = 8 (GG4) can have a minor component of Gleason pattern 5 (≤ 5% pattern 5 and > 95% pattern 4) under ISUP 2019 recommendations. In contrast, according to the GUPS guidelines, such a tumour would be scored 4 + 5 = 9 (GG5).

title: Key differences between ISUP 2019 and GUPS 2019 recommendations on Gleason grading
tablehtml:
Issue

ISUP 2019 {32459716}

GUPS 2019 {32589068}

Supporting evidence

Whether to include IDC-P admixed with invasion cancer in Gleason scoringa

Yes, incorporate into Gleason score

No, do not incorporate into Gleason score

Overall evidence for or against inclusion is inconclusive; positions were based largely on consensus opinion

 

Often cannot reliably identify IDC-P without using IHC to identify basal cells; therefore, historical and contemporary outcome data are based on incorporation of IDC-P

Cases where the presence of IDC-P would alter the Gleason score represent a small subset of these cohorts and any effect of inclusion on outcome predictions would not be apparent

Few studies have been specifically designed to address the questions of whether to include IDC-P in Gleason score / grade group and what its relationship is to outcome {31025722; 31439369}

One 2020 study showed that incorporating IDC-P made minimal difference to Gleason score assignment in biopsy and prostatectomy cohorts {32542746}; another smaller 2020 study showed that it did change in Gleason score in a significant minority (23%) of biopsy cases {32358793}

 

Avoids need for widespread IHC whenever cribriform glands or comedocarcinoma is present

Can be mitigated by performing IHC to identify IDC-P only if the result would change the Gleason score

Few studies address the question of how frequently IHC is required in diagnostic practice for the identification of IDC-P {31876580; 32358793; 32542746}

Most comedocarcinomas (Gleason pattern 5) represent IDC-P, once IHC is performed for basal cells {30720899; 29878934}

Limited data on how these differences might affect other recommendations, e.g. quantification of percentage of Gleason pattern 4 in Gleason score 7 cases {31876580; 32542746}

 

Precursor-like IDC-P associated with invasive carcinoma is so rare that its potential incorporation into Gleason score is not a major issue

Could lead to incorporation of precursor-like IDC-P into the Gleason score, thereby including an in situ component in the grade

Few published cases of precursor-like IDC-P {17617002; 20723921; 24966964; 26076065}

Recognition of minor/tertiary Gleason patterns in radical prostatectomy cases with Gleason scores of 3 + 3 = 6 and 4 + 4 = 8

Yes: if a higher grade component represents ≤ 5%b of tumour volume it is not included in the Gleason score but reported as a minor high-grade pattern

No: by GUPS definition, minor tertiary pattern 5 does not exist in these grading scenarios

Mixed evidence, data not conclusive; complicated by different grading definitions, relatively small case numbers, different endpoints

 

 

 

Specific ISUP scoring scenarios:

·         3 + 3 = 6 with minor pattern 4 (≤ 5%)

Outcome similar to that for 3 + 3 = 6 {18718699; 21933333; 24518778}

Intermediate outcome {10757404; 19683280}

Outcome similar to that for 3 + 4 = 7 {21316989}

·         3 + 3 = 6 with minor pattern 5 (≤ 5%)

Small numbers, potentially poor reproducibility {25929349}

·         4 + 4 = 8 with minor pattern 5

Outcome similar to that for 4 + 4 = 8 {10757404; 15104304}

Intermediate outcome {19683280}

Outcome similar to that for 4 + 5 = 9 {27993581}

GUPS, Genitourinary Pathology Society; IDC-P, intraductal carcinoma of the prostate; IHC, immunohistochemistry; ISUP, International Society of Urological Pathology.

aBoth organizations agree that pure IDC-P (without associated invasive carcinoma) should not be graded. bBased on the cut-off value specified in Table 2 of the ISUP 2019 paper {32459716}.

title: Differential diagnosis of benign and malignant conditions from prostatic acinar adenocarcinoma
tablehtml:
Type

Conditions and affected structures

Normal structures
 

Normal structures inside the prostate

Verumontanum, ejaculatory duct, central zone, ganglia, paraganglia, prostatic urethral urothelium
 

Normal structures outside the prostate

Seminal vesicle, Cowper gland, ganglia, paraganglia, colonic mucosa (transrectal) or skin adnexa (transperineal biopsies)

Benign prostatic lesions

 

Atrophic lesions

Simple atrophy, partial atrophy, sclerosing atrophy, proliferative inflammatory atrophy
 

Hyperplastic lesions

Adenosis (atypical adenomatous hyperplasia), sclerosing adenosis, basal cell hyperplasia, clear cell cribriform hyperplasia, postatrophic hyperplasia, verumontanum mucosal hyperplasia
 

Metaplastic lesions

Nephrogenic adenoma (nephrogenic metaplasia), mucinous metaplasia, intestinal metaplasia, urothelial metaplasia, mesonephric remnant metaplasia, squamous metaplasia
 

Inflammatory lesions

Nonspecific granulomatous prostatitis, other granulomatous inflammations, acute or chronic inflammation–associated epithelial changes
 

Treatment-related reactive changes

Postirradiation changes, androgen deprivation–induced changes, necrosis-induced changes
 

Other reactive changes

Infarct-associated epithelial changes, reactive epithelial atypia

Malignant neoplasms in the prostate

 

Different types of prostatic carcinoma

Ductal adenocarcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, sarcomatoid carcinoma, and others
 

Other carcinomas (primary or metastatic)

Urothelial carcinoma, enteric-type adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, SCNEC, LCNEC, well-differentiated NEC
 

Other malignancies (primary or metastatic)

Melanoma, sarcomas (e.g. synovial sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma), lymphomas, desmoplastic small round cell tumour, Ewing sarcoma / primitive neuroectodermal tumour
 

Metastatic carcinoma

Lung adenocarcinoma, colonic adenocarcinoma, and others

Other neoplastic conditions in the prostate
 

 

High-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia, paraganglioma

 

LCNEC, large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma; NEC, neuroendocrine carcinoma; SCNEC, small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma.

title: Diagnostic criteria for prostatic acinar adenocarcinoma
tablehtml:
Essential:

Malignant glands infiltrating the stroma

AND

An absence of basal cells (typically)

AND

Nuclear features including enlargement and hyperchromasia

 

Desirable:

 

Cytoplasmic features including amphophilic or abundant pale cytoplasm with straight luminal borders

 

Prominent nucleoli

 

Atypical luminal contents, crystalloids, blue-tinged mucin, and amorphous pink secretion

 

Perineural invasion, particularly circumferential, and intraneural invasion (specific but not sensitive)

 

Mucinous fibroplasia (specific but not sensitive)

 

Glomerulations (specific but not sensitive)
